evidence: Cic. Tusc. 2.35: Labor est fūnctiō quaedam vel animī vel corporis (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Work that costs effort and tires, of body or mind; Cicero sets it apart from pain, dolor (Tusc. 2.35). It also means hardship and trouble, and the result of toil (Lewis & Short). For effort in the sense of pains taken, see effort (opera). An old nominative labōs is in Plautus, Terence and Sallust.

evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.3.121: sēsē sibi labōrāre (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Also to take pains over something (labōrāre ut), and to be in difficulty or suffer: ex pedibus labōrāre, to have trouble with one’s feet (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: work given or sold; manual labour
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.150: quōrum operae, nōn quōrum artēs emuntur (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Work as a service rendered, especially the hired hand’s labour as against a skill; in the plural also the labourers themselves, “hands” (Lewis & Short). Its everyday sense is effort, pains (see effort).

phrases.latin: Labor est fūnctiō quaedam vel animī vel corporis, gravioris operis et mūneris.
phrases.english: Labour is a kind of exertion of mind or body in some heavier task or duty.

phrases.latin: ut ingenium est omnium hominum ā labōre prōclīve ad libīdinem
phrases.english: as every man’s nature slides away from work towards pleasure

phrases.latin: illīberālēs et sordidī quaestūs mercēnāriōrum omnium, quōrum operae, nōn quōrum artēs emuntur
phrases.english: ungentlemanly and mean are the earnings of all hired workers, whose labour is bought, not their skill

phrases.latin: canta, sed ambulā: labōrem cōnsōlāre cantandō
phrases.english: sing, but keep walking: comfort your toil with singing
